zh.q: 图上一条条标着 1010、1008 的线，是什么？
zh.concl: 等压线是同一高度上气压相等的点的连线。单位距离间的气压差叫气压梯度：间距 200 km、相邻两条差 2 hPa，梯度就是 1.0 hPa/(100 km)。
points: 等压线是同一高度上气压相等的点的连线（教材原句）。
同一张盘上的等压线标的是同一层的气压：近地面盘左 1010 → 右 1000 hPa，高空盘左 500 → 右 490 hPa，相邻两条差 2 hPa（示意）。
单位距离间的气压差叫气压梯度；参考工况间距 200 km、相邻差 2 hPa，梯度是 1.0 hPa/(100 km)。

zh.q: 只有气压梯度力的时候，风往哪里吹？
zh.concl: 水平气压梯度力垂直于等压线、由高压指向低压。如果没有其他外力，风向就与它同向——这是形成风的直接原因。
points: 水平气压梯度力的方向垂直于等压线，由高压指向低压（这盘上就是从左边高压指向右边低压，屏幕上「指右」）。
只要水平面上存在气压梯度，这个力就存在；它是形成风的直接原因。
教材图 2.14 画的是「假设没有其他外力」的情形：风向与梯度力同向，两支箭头叠在一起。

zh.q: 风一旦吹起来，为什么又被拧了一下？
zh.concl: 地球自转让运动的空气不断向右（南半球向左）偏：风向从垂直等压线开始，被地转偏向力一点点拧过去，最后与等压线平行。地转偏向力始终垂直于风向，只改变风向、不改变风速大小。
points: 风一旦形成，马上受到地转偏向力作用，风向逐渐偏离气压梯度力的方向（教材图 2.15 画的正是这个「逐渐」的过程）。
北半球风向向右偏转，南半球向左偏转。
地转偏向力始终垂直于风向（每个位置上的直角），只改变风向，不改变风速大小。

zh.q: 高空的风，为什么一直沿着等压线吹？
zh.concl: 高空没有摩擦力：水平气压梯度力与地转偏向力大小相等、方向相反，风不再偏转，风向最终与等压线平行。
points: 高空不受摩擦力，只剩水平气压梯度力与地转偏向力两个力。
两力大小相等、方向相反（盘面上两支箭头等长反向），风就稳定下来不再偏。
结果：风向最终与等压线平行（教材图 2.15 最后那个位置）。

zh.q: 贴地这一层，风为什么又斜了？
zh.concl: 近地面还要受摩擦力：摩擦力与风向相反、减小风速。三个力共同作用下，风向与等压线斜交，并指向低压一侧。
points: 近地面还受摩擦力：地面和空气之间、运动状况不同的空气层之间相互作用产生的阻力。
摩擦力与风向相反，对风有阻碍作用，可以减小风速。
三力共同作用下风向与等压线斜交（教材图 2.16），但仍指向低压一侧：参考工况 31°。

zh.q: 同样的气压场，南半球的风吹向哪边？
zh.concl: 同一气压场上，北半球的风向右偏、南半球向左偏：风向镜像到另一侧，风速与等压线夹角都不变。
points: 同一气压场上，北半球风向偏右、南半球风向偏左。
画面里整串箭头镜像过去：北半球最后一支指向屏幕下方（南），南半球指向屏幕上方（北），风速与夹角不变。
判读口诀：背风而立，北半球低压在左、高压在右，南半球相反。

zh.q: 等压线挤在一起的地方，风为什么更大？
zh.concl: 等压线越密，气压梯度越大，风力越大；判风向仍按「北半球右偏、斜穿等压线指向低压」。
points: 等压线的疏密程度反映了气压梯度的大小，等压线越密，气压梯度越大（教材 p.40 原句）。
教材 p.40 活动里甲（蒙古东部，等压线密）与乙（四川盆地南缘，等压线稀）就是这样比的。

zh.q: 考核：让风速 ≥ 12 m/s，风向贴近等压线
zh.concl: 风的大小与方向由气压梯度和摩擦力共同决定：等压线越密、地面越光滑，风越大、越接近平行等压线。
points: 先把「等压线间距」拖小：气压梯度变大，风就变大。
再把「摩擦系数」拖小：摩擦力减小，风向更贴近等压线。
半球必须是北半球——南半球风向镜像，按本关的判据不算达标。

en.q: What are the lines on the map labeled 1010, 1008 and so on?
en.concl: Isobars are lines joining points of equal pressure at the same altitude. The pressure difference per unit distance is the pressure gradient: with 200 km spacing and 2 hPa between neighboring lines, the gradient is 1.0 hPa/(100 km).
points: Isobars are lines joining points of equal pressure at the same altitude (textbook wording).
The isobars on one disk give the pressure at one level: surface disk 1010 on the left → 1000 hPa on the right, upper-air disk 500 → 490 hPa, 2 hPa between neighbors (schematic).
The pressure difference per unit distance is the pressure gradient; in the reference case the spacing is 200 km and neighbors differ by 2 hPa, so the gradient is 1.0 hPa/(100 km).

en.q: With only the pressure gradient force, which way does the wind blow?
en.concl: The horizontal pressure gradient force is perpendicular to the isobars and points from high to low pressure. Without other forces the wind would blow in the same direction; it is the direct cause of wind.
points: The horizontal pressure gradient force is perpendicular to the isobars and points from high to low pressure (on this disk from high on the left to low on the right, "pointing right" on screen).
Wherever there is a pressure gradient on a horizontal plane, this force exists; it is the direct cause of wind.
Textbook Fig. 2.14 shows the case "assuming no other forces": the wind is in the same direction as the gradient force and the two arrows overlap.

en.q: Once the wind starts blowing, why does it get twisted?
en.concl: Earth's rotation keeps deflecting moving air to the right (left in the Southern Hemisphere): the wind starts perpendicular to the isobars, is twisted bit by bit by the Coriolis force and ends parallel to them. The Coriolis force is always perpendicular to the wind and changes only its direction, not its speed.
points: As soon as wind forms it is acted on by the Coriolis force, and its direction gradually departs from that of the pressure gradient force (Fig. 2.15 shows exactly this gradual process).
In the Northern Hemisphere the wind is deflected to the right, in the Southern Hemisphere to the left.
The Coriolis force is always perpendicular to the wind (the right angle at each position) and changes only the direction, not the speed.

en.q: Why does upper-air wind keep blowing along the isobars?
en.concl: There is no friction aloft: the horizontal pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force are equal and opposite, the wind stops deflecting and ends up parallel to the isobars.
points: Aloft there is no friction, only the horizontal pressure gradient force and the Coriolis force.
The two forces are equal and opposite (two arrows of equal length pointing opposite ways on the disk), so the wind settles and stops deflecting.
Result: the wind ends up parallel to the isobars (the last position in Fig. 2.15).

en.q: In the layer next to the ground, why is the wind oblique again?
en.concl: Near the surface there is also friction, opposite the wind, reducing its speed. Under the three forces together the wind crosses the isobars obliquely, toward the low-pressure side.
points: Near the surface there is also friction: resistance from the interaction between the ground and the air, and between layers of air moving differently.
Friction is opposite the wind, hinders it and reduces wind speed.
Under the three forces the wind crosses the isobars obliquely (textbook Fig. 2.16), but still toward the low-pressure side: 31° in the reference case.

en.q: With the same pressure field, which way does the wind blow in the Southern Hemisphere?
en.concl: In the same pressure field, wind deflects right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern: the direction mirrors to the other side while wind speed and angle to the isobars stay the same.
points: In the same pressure field, wind deflects right in the Northern Hemisphere and left in the Southern.
The whole series of arrows mirrors on screen: in the north the last arrow points to the bottom of the screen (south), in the south to the top (north); wind speed and angle are unchanged.
Rule of thumb: stand with your back to the wind; in the Northern Hemisphere low pressure is on your left and high on your right, the reverse in the south.

en.q: Why is the wind stronger where the isobars are crowded together?
en.concl: The denser the isobars, the larger the pressure gradient and the stronger the wind; wind direction is still judged by "deflects right in the north, crosses isobars obliquely toward low pressure".
points: The spacing of isobars reflects the size of the pressure gradient; the denser the isobars, the larger the gradient (textbook p.40 wording).
Spacing 300→100 km: gradient 0.7→2.0 hPa/(100 km), wind 5.1→15.2 m/s.
The textbook p.40 activity compares Jia (eastern Mongolia, dense isobars) and Yi (southern edge of the Sichuan Basin, sparse isobars) in exactly this way.

en.q: Assessment: get wind ≥ 12 m/s blowing close to the isobars
en.concl: Wind strength and direction are set jointly by the pressure gradient and friction: the denser the isobars and smoother the ground, the stronger the wind and the closer it is to parallel with the isobars.
points: First drag "Isobar spacing" down: the pressure gradient grows and the wind strengthens.
Then drag "Friction coefficient" down: friction decreases and the wind lies closer to the isobars.
The hemisphere must be northern; in the south the wind direction mirrors and doesn't count by this level's criteria.
